topic: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
subject: physics

items.q: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of another. What happens?
items.correct: They repel each other, because the poles are alike
items.misconception: They attract each other, because magnets attract
items.why: Almost every everyday encounter with a magnet is an attraction: fridge magnets, magnetic catches, picking up paperclips. Repulsion is only felt when a student deliberately turns one magnet round. Whether the force is a push or a pull depends only on which poles face each other. Like poles (N–N or S–S) repel; unlike poles (N–S) attract. Both are equally normal magnetic behaviour.
items.random_wrong: Nothing happens until the magnets are touching

items.q: Why is the repulsion between two north poles described as a non-contact force?
items.correct: The magnets push apart without ever touching
items.misconception: The magnets touch each other, then spring apart
items.why: Most forces a student has met push or pull through contact, and the magnetic force is only obvious in the last centimetre or two, so it looks as though contact starts it. The force acts across the gap. Bring two north poles slowly together and the push is felt before they meet, growing as the distance falls. That is what makes it a non-contact force.
items.random_wrong: The push is really an attraction seen in reverse

items.q: Where on a bar magnet are the magnetic forces strongest?
items.correct: At the two poles, at the ends of the magnet
items.misconception: In the middle, exactly midway between the poles
items.why: 'Strongest in the middle' matches everyday ideas about the centre of an object being the heart of it, and a bar magnet looks uniform, so nothing on it marks the ends out. The poles are by definition the places where the magnetic forces are strongest, and they are at the ends. Hold a paperclip against the middle of a bar magnet and it barely holds; hold it at an end and it grips.
items.random_wrong: At the north pole only, not at the south pole

items.q: Which statement describes a permanent magnet?
items.correct: It produces its own magnetic field at all times
items.misconception: It becomes magnetic only when another magnet is near
items.why: A chain of paperclips hanging from a magnet looks like each clip has been turned into a magnet, and steel objects that have been stroked with a magnet do keep a little magnetism. The clips are induced magnets: they are only magnetic while they sit in the magnet's field. Take the magnet away and the chain falls apart, because an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly. Only a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.
items.random_wrong: It is any metal, since all metals produce fields

items.q: A steel paperclip hangs from one pole of a bar magnet. The magnet is then taken away. What happens to the paperclip's magnetism?
items.correct: It loses most or all of its magnetism quickly
items.misconception: It stays a magnet permanently from then on
items.why: A chain of paperclips hanging from a magnet looks like each clip has been turned into a magnet, and steel objects that have been stroked with a magnet do keep a little magnetism. The clips are induced magnets: they are only magnetic while they sit in the magnet's field. Take the magnet away and the chain falls apart, because an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly. Only a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.
items.random_wrong: It loses its magnetism only when it is heated

items.q: What is the key difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?
items.correct: Only the permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field
items.misconception: Only the induced magnet is able to lose its magnetism
items.why: A chain of paperclips hanging from a magnet looks like each clip has been turned into a magnet, and steel objects that have been stroked with a magnet do keep a little magnetism. The clips are induced magnets: they are only magnetic while they sit in the magnet's field. Take the magnet away and the chain falls apart, because an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly. Only a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.
items.random_wrong: Only the induced magnet can both attract and repel

items.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is held close to an unmagnetised iron nail. What force acts on the nail?
items.correct: Attraction, because induced magnetism always attracts
items.misconception: Repulsion, because the nail is induced as a north pole
items.why: Students correctly learn that like poles repel, then apply it to induction without asking which way round the poles are induced. The material is always induced with the unlike pole facing the magnet, so the result is always attraction. The specification is absolute here: induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, and the force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
items.random_wrong: None at all, until the nail has been magnetised

items.q: Which list contains only magnetic materials?
items.correct: Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel
items.misconception: Iron, copper, cobalt and nickel
items.why: The rule 'magnets stick to metal, not to plastic or wood' works for almost every classroom object, because most of the metal objects in a classroom are steel. Only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are magnetic materials. A magnet will not attract a copper coin or an aluminium can, even though both are metals.
items.random_wrong: Iron, steel, aluminium and nickel

items.q: What is meant by the magnetic field of a magnet?
items.correct: The region where it exerts a force on magnetic materials
items.misconception: The set of lines that have been drawn around the magnet
items.why: Iron filings gather into visible strands with visible gaps, and every textbook diagram shows a fixed number of separate lines, which makes the lines look like real objects. Field lines are a model. The field exists everywhere around the magnet and fades gradually with distance rather than stopping at an edge. How closely the lines are drawn is the code for how strong the field is: close together means strong.
items.random_wrong: The region right at the centre of the magnet only

items.q: A bar magnet is brought close to a piece of unmagnetised cobalt. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Both poles of the magnet attract the cobalt
items.misconception: The north pole attracts it, the south repels it
items.why: Students correctly learn that like poles repel, then apply it to induction without asking which way round the poles are induced. The material is always induced with the unlike pole facing the magnet, so the result is always attraction. The specification is absolute here: induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, and the force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
items.random_wrong: Neither pole affects it until it is magnetised

items.q: A plotting compass is moved from close to a bar magnet to much further away. What happens to the strength of the field at the compass?
items.correct: It gets weaker as the compass moves away
items.misconception: It stays the same all round the magnet
items.why: Magnets are described in everyday language as 'strong' or 'weak' as if strength were a single property of the object rather than something that varies from point to point. Field strength is a property of each point in the field. It falls as the distance from the magnet increases, and it is greatest at the poles, which is why field lines are drawn closest together there.
items.random_wrong: It falls to zero outside the drawn lines

items.q: On a correctly drawn field pattern of a bar magnet, where are the field lines closest together?
items.correct: Near the poles, where the field is strongest
items.misconception: Near the middle, where the magnet is thickest
items.why: 'Strongest in the middle' matches everyday ideas about the centre of an object being the heart of it, and a bar magnet looks uniform, so nothing on it marks the ends out. The poles are by definition the places where the magnetic forces are strongest, and they are at the ends. Hold a paperclip against the middle of a bar magnet and it barely holds; hold it at an end and it grips.
items.random_wrong: Far from the magnet, where the field is weaker

items.q: Which statement about the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet is correct?
items.correct: They are drawn from the north pole to the south pole
items.misconception: They are drawn from the south pole to the north pole
items.why: Students associate north with the 'main' or 'positive' end of a magnet, and arrows are often read as pointing to where something is heading rather than away from where it starts. Outside the magnet the lines run from north to south. It follows from the definition of field direction: a free north pole placed near the magnet's north pole would be pushed away from it and towards the south pole.
items.random_wrong: They point the way a south pole would be pushed

items.q: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point defined?
items.correct: By the force that would act on a north pole there
items.misconception: By the force that would act on a south pole there
items.why: The convention is arbitrary from the student's point of view, so there is nothing to hold it in place unless it is tied to the north-to-south rule for field lines. The convention is fixed: field direction is the direction of the force on another north pole placed at that point. A south pole would be pushed the opposite way, so using it would reverse every arrow.
items.random_wrong: By where the drawn lines are closest together

items.q: What does a magnetic compass contain?
items.correct: A small bar magnet on a free pivot
items.misconception: A small piece of unmagnetised iron
items.why: The needle is small, grey and metallic, and induced magnetism does make iron line up in a field, so the wrong explanation still predicts the right movement in some situations. The needle is a small bar magnet with its own north and south pole. That is why it settles pointing one specific way rather than either way round: the field turns its north pole in a definite direction.
items.random_wrong: A small piece of copper on a pivot

items.q: Well away from any other magnet, a compass needle always settles pointing the same way. What does this show?
items.correct: The Earth produces a magnetic field of its own
items.misconception: The needle is pulled round by the Earth's gravity
items.why: Gravity and rotation are the two things students already know the Earth does to objects, so they are reached for first when the Earth is said to affect something. Gravity pulls the needle down, not round, and it would act on any needle, magnetised or not. Only a magnetic field can turn a magnet, so the compass shows that the Earth has a magnetic field.
items.random_wrong: The needle is not a magnet, it simply lines up

items.q: A student is asked to plot the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Which method is correct?
items.correct: Mark a dot at each end of the needle, move the compass on to the last dot and repeat
items.misconception: Sprinkle iron filings over the magnet and draw arrows along the lines they form
items.why: The filing pattern is far more striking than a compass plot and appears instantly, so it looks like the complete answer. Each filing becomes an induced magnet and lines up along the field, but it has no arrow: a filing pointing along a line looks the same either way round. The specification asks for the pattern to be plotted with a compass, whose needle gives the direction as well as the line.
items.random_wrong: Draw a straight line from the north pole across to the south pole of the magnet

items.q: Which features must a correctly drawn field pattern for a bar magnet show?
items.correct: Curved lines with arrows, packed closest at the poles
items.misconception: Evenly spaced lines all round, each with an arrow on it
items.why: Iron filings gather into visible strands with visible gaps, and every textbook diagram shows a fixed number of separate lines, which makes the lines look like real objects. Field lines are a model. The field exists everywhere around the magnet and fades gradually with distance rather than stopping at an edge. How closely the lines are drawn is the code for how strong the field is: close together means strong.
items.random_wrong: Curved lines with arrows running from south pole to north

items.q: How is the behaviour of a magnetic compass evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic?
items.correct: A compass lines up with a field produced inside the Earth
items.misconception: A compass points to the magnetic rocks in the ground below
items.why: Students know some rocks are magnetic, and a local explanation feels safer than claiming something about a part of the Earth nobody has ever seen. Surface rocks vary from place to place, so they could not turn every compass on Earth the same consistent way. A field that acts over the whole planet must be produced deep inside it, which is the evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.
items.random_wrong: A compass is pulled towards the North Pole by gravity there

items.q: Two bar magnets are placed end to end and pull towards each other. What must be true of the facing poles?
items.correct: They are unlike: one north and one south
items.misconception: They are alike, because like poles attract
items.why: Almost every everyday encounter with a magnet is an attraction: fridge magnets, magnetic catches, picking up paperclips. Repulsion is only felt when a student deliberately turns one magnet round. Whether the force is a push or a pull depends only on which poles face each other. Like poles (N–N or S–S) repel; unlike poles (N–S) attract. Both are equally normal magnetic behaviour.
items.random_wrong: One is a magnet, one an induced south pole

items.q: What shape are the field lines around a bar magnet?
items.correct: Smooth curves that leave the north pole and loop round to the south pole, closest together at the poles.
items.misconception: You draw straight lines from the north pole across to the south pole, evenly spaced, like the rungs of a ladder.
items.why: Straight lines are quicker to draw, and students who see the lines as a way of joining the two poles rather than as a map of the field see no reason for them to bend or bunch. The pattern must show how strength and direction change from one point to another: lines curve outwards from the north pole and round into the south pole, and they crowd together near the poles where the field is strongest, spreading out where it is weaker.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the north pole of a magnet stronger than the south pole?
items.correct: No. Both poles are places where the magnetic forces are strongest.
items.misconception: North is the working end of a magnet — it is the one that attracts and the one the field comes out of, so it must be the stronger pole.
items.why: Field lines are drawn leaving the north pole, and the north pole is always named first, both of which make north look like the active end. The two poles of a magnet are equally strong. A paperclip is held just as firmly at the south end as at the north, and the lines that leave the north pole are exactly the ones that enter the south pole.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.7.1 Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
